summary: This Wikipedia article describes the common cold, a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract caused mainly by rhinoviruses, with over 200 viral types implicated. It covers symptoms and progression, transmission, pathophysiology, diagnosis, prevention, management (including zinc, vitamins C and D, and alternative medicine), prognosis, epidemiology, the weather-seasonality misconception, history, research directions, and economic impact. The note emphasizes that there is no vaccine or cure, and that symptomatic treatment and hand washing are the main approaches.
one_line: Overview of the common cold: a viral upper respiratory infection, its causes, transmission, symptoms, evidence-based treatments, history, and economic impact.
key_facts: The common cold is a viral infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract that primarily affects the respiratory mucosa of the nose, throat, sinuses, and larynx.
Symptoms usually appear fewer than two days after exposure to the virus and people usually recover in seven to ten days, though some symptoms may last up to three weeks.
Rhinoviruses are the most commonly implicated cause of colds, found in 30–80% of cases, and more than 200 viral types are associated with colds.
Antibiotics should not be used for colds because all colds are caused by viruses.
There is no vaccine for the common cold, and vaccination has proven difficult because there are many viruses involved and they mutate rapidly.
Zinc supplements may shorten the duration of colds by up to 33% if supplementation begins within 24 hours of symptom onset.
Routine vitamin C supplements do not reduce the risk or severity of the common cold, though they may reduce its duration.
In the United States, the common cold leads to 75–100 million physician visits annually at a conservative cost estimate of $7.7 billion per year.
Adults get two to three colds a year on average, while children may get six to eight.
The name 'cold' came into use in the 16th century, due to the similarity between its symptoms and those of exposure to cold weather.
The Common Cold Unit (CCU) was set up by the Medical Research Council in 1946 in the United Kingdom, and rhinovirus was discovered there in 1956.
The Common Cold Unit was closed in 1989, two years after it completed research of zinc gluconate lozenges.
The symptoms of the common cold are believed to be primarily related to the immune response to the virus rather than tissue destruction.
Rhinovirus-caused colds are most infectious during the first three days of symptoms.
The Egyptian Ebers papyrus, written before the 16th century BCE, describes the symptoms and treatment of the common cold.

entities.role: body that set up the Common Cold Unit in the United Kingdom in 1946

entities.name: Ebers papyrus
entities.role: Egyptian medical text, described as the oldest existing medical text, that describes the symptoms and treatment of colds

entities.role: antiviral drug under trial that shows promise against picornaviruses

entities.role: antiviral drug being trialed for the common cold

entities.role: heated and humidified air device whose benefit as of 2017 is of unclear benefit

entities.name: Adelaide Island
entities.role: location of a British scientific base where an outbreak of colds occurred after seventeen weeks of isolation
